claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization sequence.
Several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases form during solidification under standard cooling protocols.
A brief isothermal hold slightly below Tg immediately after rapid quenching will enhance amorphous retention.
The post-quench sub-Tg hold will improve the alloy's thermal stability.
The post-quench sub-Tg hold suppresses the kinetics of primary crystallization.
The intervention consists of a brief isothermal hold at Tg minus a small temperature offset, applied immediately after rapid quenching and before controlled reheating.
The initial cooling rate must exceed the critical cooling-rate boundary associated with primary crystallization.
The appropriate hold duration is likely on the order of seconds.
The sub-Tg hold enhances short-range structural ordering within the amorphous matrix.
Enhanced short-range ordering resists nucleation of crystalline phases.
Sub-Tg annealing permits structural relaxation and reduces internal stresses.
Structural relaxation reduces atomic mobility and lowers the driving force for primary crystallization during reheating.
The thermal treatment retards diffusion pathways required for crystalline nucleation and growth.
Relative to continuous rapid quenching followed by standard reheating, the hold will increase the retained amorphous fraction.
Relative to the control, the hold will shift exothermic crystallization peaks to higher temperatures.
Standard rapid cooling followed by slower cooling or direct reheating produces early primary crystallization and multiple non-eutectic phases.
The beneficial effect requires an ultrafast cooling rate that bypasses extensive nucleation and a hold temperature narrowly below Tg.
A hold temperature that is too high or too low, or a hold that is excessively long, may provide inadequate relaxation or trigger crystallization.
